newsitem.title: GERMANY: German equity buybacks unlikely until 1998.
newsitem.headline: German equity buybacks unlikely until 1998.

text.p: One thing guaranteed to bring a smile to a shareholder's face is a company share buyback, but legal restrictions look set to keep these a virtual impossibility in Germany at least until 1998.

German companies, fresh converts to shareholder value, are lobbying for a relaxation of the rules which restrict buybacks to emergency situations, but infant reform plans in Bonn are proceeding painfully slowly.
"Nothing much will change in this regard before 1998," a Justice Ministry official said, noting that the necessary changes had not even reached a draft proposal stage.

Top German industrialists, notably chemicals group BASF AG's chief financial officer Max Dietrich Kley, have argued for years that buybacks are an effective means of rewarding shareholders and tackling excess liquidity.

Lobby groups,including the German Share Institute, are also pushing to have buybacks made easier, since the mere announcement that a company intends buying a large chunk of its own equity is generally enough to send its stock price surging.
Unlike dividend payments, any capital gains shareholders accrue are tax free under current German law, provided the share is held for more than six months.
Government stock market experts are also keen to liberalise current laws, which allow companies to buy their own stock only to avert serious and imminent damage to their business.
A recent paper suggested adapting the law to correspond with a 1976 EU directive, which would permit firms to buy back up to 10 percent of their own capital.
The Justice Ministry says the proposals may be dicussed in a government committee on November 6 but that any change in the law could not take effect before January 1 1998.
Some lobbyists say the suggested reforms do not go far enough.

Paul Berwein, an official stock broker at the Munich exchange, has set up a lobby group which is urging the government to allow firms to buy back their shares from individual stockholders as well as on the open market.

Describing the suggested 10 percent buyback allowance as a "minimum solution", Berwein's group believes its suggestion would help explode the much-criticised cross-shareholdings between German banks and industrial companies.
Critics of the reform complain that share buybacks can undermine creditors because of the resulting reduction in a company's base capital.
Opponents also worry that company heads could try to use the buyback option to outmanoeuvre opposing shareholders or privilege others.
Finally, German insider trading laws forbid management board members from getting involved in equity transactions, making the whole buyback issue problematic.
However, Berwein's group has suggested various ways to minimise these risks.
First, companies would have to build reserves in order to finance buy-backs without reducing their base capital.
In addition, buybacks would have to be approved by the annual shareholder meeting and the shares bought back would not carry voting rights.

The group has also proposed that companies not be allowed to pay more than a 10 percent premium on the market value of a share package bought from a single investor. If such packages were sold onward, the price could be no less than five percent below the market value.
